title: IX. The Devil. Ivan’s Nightmare
paragraphs: I am not a doctor, but I feel the time has come to give the reader some account of Ivan’s illness. I can say one thing in advance: at that moment he was on the very eve of an attack of brain fever. His health had been poor for a long time, but it had stubbornly resisted the fever, which in the end overpowered it. I know nothing of medicine, so take this as a guess. By a terrible effort of will he had perhaps managed to put the attack off for a while, hoping, of course, to beat it altogether. He knew he was unwell. But he hated the thought of being ill at that fatal time, at the approaching crisis of his life, when he needed all his wits about him, to say what he had to say boldly and firmly and “to justify himself to himself.”

He had, however, gone to see the new doctor, the one brought from Moscow on Katerina Ivanovna’s fantastic notion, which I have mentioned already. The doctor listened to him and examined him. He decided that Ivan really did have some disorder of the brain, and he was not at all surprised by something Ivan admitted to him with reluctance. “Hallucinations are quite likely in your condition,” the doctor said, “though it would be better to check them ... You must take steps at once, without losing a moment, or things will go badly for you.” But Ivan ignored this sensible advice and did not take to his bed to be nursed. “I’m walking about, so I’m strong enough. If I drop, it will be different. Then anyone who likes can nurse me,” he decided, and that was the end of it.

And so he sat there, almost aware of his own delirium and, as I have said already, staring fixedly at something on the sofa against the opposite wall. Someone seemed to be sitting there. Goodness knows how he had got in, for he had not been in the room when Ivan came back from Smerdyakov’s. He was a man, or more exactly a Russian gentleman of a particular kind, no longer young, _qui faisait la cinquantaine_, as the French say. His dark hair was rather long and still thick, with a little gray in it, and he had a small pointed beard. He wore a brownish reefer jacket, rather shabby, though plainly cut by a good tailor. The style was at least three years old, and smart, well-to-do people had given it up two years before. His shirt and his long scarf-like necktie were the sort worn by people who want to look stylish, but a closer look showed the shirt was none too clean and the wide scarf was badly worn. The visitor’s check trousers were excellently cut, but they were too light in color and too tight for the present fashion. His soft, fluffy white hat was wrong for the season.

In short, he gave every appearance of gentility on a small income. He seemed to belong to the class of idle landowners who flourished in the days of serfdom. He had clearly moved in good, fashionable society at some time and had once had good connections, which he might even have kept. But after a gay youth he had slowly grown poor when serfdom was abolished, and he had sunk to the position of a poor relation of the best sort. He drifted from one good old friend to the next. They took him in because he was companionable and easygoing, and because he was, after all, a gentleman who could be asked to sit down with anyone, though not, of course, in the place of honor. Such obliging gentlemen in dependent positions can tell a story and make a fourth at cards, and they strongly dislike having any duties forced on them. They are usually solitary creatures, bachelors or widowers. Sometimes they have children, but the children are always being raised far away, at some aunt’s, and these gentlemen never mention the aunt in good society, as if ashamed of the connection. Little by little they lose sight of their children altogether, though now and then they get a birthday or Christmas letter from them and sometimes even answer it.

The face of the unexpected visitor was not so much good-natured as obliging, ready to put on any pleasant expression as the occasion called for it. He had no watch, but he did have a tortoise-shell lorgnette on a black ribbon. On the middle finger of his right hand was a heavy gold ring set with a cheap opal.

Ivan was angrily silent and would not start the conversation. The visitor waited. He sat exactly like a poor relation who has come down from his room to keep his host company over tea, and who stays discreetly quiet because his host is frowning and lost in thought. But he was ready for any friendly chat the moment his host began one. Suddenly his face showed concern.

“I say,” he began, turning to Ivan, “forgive me, I only mention it to remind you. You went to Smerdyakov’s to find out about Katerina Ivanovna, and you came away without learning a thing about her. You probably forgot—”

“Ah, yes,” broke from Ivan, and his face clouded with uneasiness. “Yes, I forgot ... but it doesn’t matter now, never mind, it can wait until tomorrow,” he muttered to himself. “And you,” he added, turning on his visitor, “I’d have remembered it myself in a minute, because that was exactly what was tormenting me! Why do you butt in? Do you want me to believe you put it into my head and I never remembered it on my own?”

“Then don’t believe it,” said the gentleman, with a friendly smile. “What’s the use of believing against your will? Besides, proofs don’t help belief, least of all material proofs. Thomas believed not because he saw Christ risen, but because he wanted to believe before he saw. Take the spiritualists, for example ... I’m very fond of them ... just think, they imagine they’re serving the cause of religion because the devils show them their horns from the other world. That, they say, is a material proof, so to speak, that there is another world. The other world and material proofs, whatever next! And if it comes to that, does proving there’s a devil prove there’s a God? I want to join an idealist society. I’ll lead the opposition in it. I’ll say I’m a realist but not a materialist, he he!”

“Listen,” Ivan said, suddenly getting up from the table. “I seem to be delirious ... in fact I am delirious. Talk whatever nonsense you like, I don’t care! You won’t drive me into a fury this time, the way you did before. But I feel somehow ashamed ... I want to walk about the room ... Sometimes I can’t see you and can’t even hear your voice, as happened last time, but I always guess what you’re rattling on about, because it’s _I myself speaking, not you_. The only thing is, I don’t know whether I was dreaming last time or really saw you. I’ll wet a towel and put it on my head, and maybe you’ll vanish into thin air.”
Ivan went to the corner, took a towel, and did as he had said. Then, with the wet towel on his head, he began pacing up and down the room.
“I’m so glad you treat me so familiarly,” the visitor began.

“Fool,” Ivan laughed, “you think I’d stand on ceremony with you? I’m in good spirits now, though my forehead hurts ... and the top of my head ... Only please don’t talk philosophy the way you did last time. If you can’t clear out, talk about something amusing. Tell me gossip. You’re a poor relation, so gossip is your line. What a nightmare to have! But I’m not afraid of you. I’ll get the better of you. They won’t put me in a madhouse!”

“_C’est charmant_, poor relation. Yes, I’m in my natural shape. What am I on earth, after all, but a poor relation? By the way, as I listen to you I’m rather surprised to find you’re actually starting to take me for something real, and not just a figment of your imagination, as you kept insisting last time—”

“Not for one minute have I taken you for real,” Ivan cried, in a sort of fury. “You’re a lie, you’re my illness, you’re a phantom. I just don’t know how to destroy you, and I see I’ll have to suffer for a while. You’re my hallucination. You’re myself in bodily form, but only one side of me ... of my thoughts and feelings, and only the nastiest and stupidest of them. Seen that way you might even interest me, if only I had time to waste on you—”

“Pardon me, pardon me, I’ll catch you out. When you flew at Alyosha under the lamp-post this evening and shouted at him, ‘You learned it from _him_! How do you know _he_ visits me?’ you were thinking of me. So for one brief moment you did believe I really exist,” the gentleman said with a bland laugh.
“Yes, that was a moment of weakness ... but I couldn’t believe in you. I don’t know if I was asleep or awake last time. Maybe I was only dreaming and never really saw you at all—”
“And why were you so short with Alyosha just now? He’s a dear. I behaved badly toward him over Father Zossima.”
“Don’t talk about Alyosha! How dare you, you lackey!” Ivan laughed again.
“You scold me, but you laugh, and that’s a good sign. Still, you’re ever so much more polite than you were last time, and I know why: that great resolution of yours—”
“Don’t speak of my resolution,” Ivan cried savagely.
“I understand, I understand, _c’est noble, c’est charmant_, you’re going to stand up for your brother and sacrifice yourself ... _C’est chevaleresque_.”
“Shut up, or I’ll kick you!”

“I won’t be wholly sorry, because then I’ll have got what I wanted. If you kick me, you have to believe I’m real, since nobody kicks ghosts. Joking aside, it makes no difference to me. Scold all you like, though it’s better to be a little more polite, even to me. ‘Fool, lackey!’ What words!”
“When I scold you, I’m scolding myself,” Ivan laughed again. “You’re me, myself, only with a different face. You say just what I’m thinking ... and you can’t say anything new!”
“If I think the way you do, that does me credit,” the gentleman declared, with delicacy and dignity.

“You pick out only my worst thoughts, and the stupid ones at that. You’re stupid and vulgar. You’re awfully stupid. No, I can’t stand you! What am I to do, what am I to do?” Ivan said through clenched teeth.

“My dear friend, above all I want to behave like a gentleman and be recognized as one,” the visitor began, in a burst of apologetic, simple-hearted pride, so typical of a poor relation. “I’m poor, but ... I won’t say very honest, but ... it’s an axiom accepted everywhere in society that I’m a fallen angel. I certainly can’t imagine how I ever was an angel. If I was, it was so long ago that there’s no harm in forgetting it. Now I only care about my reputation as a gentlemanly person, and I live as best I can, trying to be agreeable. I truly love men, I’ve been greatly slandered! When I stay with you here from time to time, my life takes on a kind of reality, and that’s what I like best. You see, like you, I suffer from the fantastic, so I love the realism of earth. Here, with you, everything has limits, everything is formulated and geometrical, while all we have are indeterminate equations! I wander about here dreaming. I like dreaming. Besides, on earth I turn superstitious. Please don’t laugh, that’s exactly what I like, turning superstitious. I take up all your habits here: I’ve grown fond of the public baths, would you believe it? I go and steam myself with merchants and priests. What I dream of is becoming incarnate once and for all, irrevocably, as some merchant’s wife weighing eighteen stone, and believing everything she believes. My ideal is to go to church and put up a candle in simple-hearted faith, on my word it is. Then my sufferings would be over. I like being doctored too. In the spring there was an outbreak of smallpox and I went and got vaccinated at a foundling hospital. If you only knew how I enjoyed myself that day! I gave ten roubles to the cause of the Slavs! ... But you’re not listening. Do you know, you’re not at all well this evening? I know you saw that doctor yesterday ... well, how is your health? What did the doctor say?”
“Fool!” Ivan snapped.
“Well, you’re clever, anyway. Scolding again? I didn’t ask out of sympathy. You needn’t answer. The rheumatism’s come back now—”
“Fool!” Ivan said again.
“You keep saying the same thing, but I had such a bad attack of rheumatism last year that I remember it to this day.”
“The devil have rheumatism!”
“Why not, if I sometimes take on fleshly form? I take on fleshly form and I take the consequences. Satan _sum et nihil humanum a me alienum puto_.”
“What, what, Satan _sum et nihil humanum_ ... that’s not bad for the devil!”
“I’m glad I’ve finally pleased you.”
“But you didn’t get that from me.” Ivan stopped suddenly, as if struck. “That never came into my head. That’s strange.”

“_C’est du nouveau, n’est-ce pas?_ This time I’ll be honest and explain it to you. Listen. In dreams, and especially in nightmares, brought on by indigestion or anything else, a man sometimes sees such artistic visions, such complex and real actuality, such events, even a whole world of events, woven into such a plot, with such unexpected details, from the loftiest matters down to the last button on a cuff, as I swear Leo Tolstoy never invented. Yet such dreams are sometimes seen not by writers but by quite ordinary people, officials, journalists, priests ... The whole matter is a complete riddle. A statesman actually confessed to me that all his best ideas came to him in his sleep. Well, it’s the same now. I may be your hallucination, but just as in a nightmare I say original things that never came into your head before. So I don’t repeat your ideas, and yet I’m only your nightmare, nothing more.”
“You’re lying. Your aim is to convince me you exist on your own and aren’t my nightmare, and now you’re saying you’re a dream.”
“My dear fellow, I’ve taken up a special method today, I’ll explain it to you later. Wait, where did I leave off? Oh, yes! I caught a cold then, only not here but over yonder.”

“Where’s yonder? Tell me, will you be here long? Can’t you go away?” Ivan exclaimed, almost in despair. He stopped pacing, sat down on the sofa, put his elbows on the table again and gripped his head tight in both hands. He pulled off the wet towel and threw it aside in annoyance. It was plainly no use.

“Your nerves are shot,” remarked the gentleman, in an easy, careless manner that was still perfectly polite. “You’re angry with me even for catching cold, though it happened in the most natural way. I was in a hurry that day. I was on my way to a diplomatic _soirée_ at the house of a high-ranking lady in Petersburg, who was angling for influence in the Ministry. So there I was in evening dress, white tie and gloves, and yet I was God knows where, and I had to fly through space to get to your earth.... It took only an instant, of course. But a ray of light from the sun takes a full eight minutes, and just picture it, in an evening suit and open waistcoat. Spirits don’t freeze, but when one’s in the flesh, well ... in short, I didn’t stop to think. I simply set off. And you know, up in those ethereal spaces, in the water above the firmament, the frost is such that ... well, you can’t even call it frost. Imagine, 150 degrees below zero! You know the game the village girls play? They invite some unsuspecting fellow to lick an ax when it’s thirty degrees below. His tongue freezes to it on the spot, and the poor dupe tears off the skin and bleeds. But that’s only at 30 degrees. At 150, I imagine, you’d just have to touch the ax with your finger and that would be the end of you ... if only there could be an ax there.”
“And can there be an ax there?” Ivan cut in, with careless contempt. He was straining with all his might not to believe in the delusion, and not to slip into complete madness.
“An ax?” the guest broke in, surprised.
“Yes! What would become of an ax up there?” Ivan cried suddenly, with a savage, dogged stubbornness.

“What would become of an ax in space? _Quelle idée!_ If it dropped some distance, I think it would simply start circling the earth, not knowing why, like a satellite. The astronomers would work out when the ax rises and sets, _Gatzuk_ would put it in his almanac, and that’s all.”

“You’re stupid, awfully stupid,” said Ivan peevishly. “Tell cleverer lies or I won’t listen. You’re trying to beat me with realism, to prove to me that you exist. But I don’t want to believe you exist! I won’t believe it!”

“But I’m not lying. Every word is true. Unfortunately the truth is hardly ever amusing. I see you keep expecting something big from me, and perhaps something fine. What a pity. I only give what I can—”
“Don’t talk philosophy, you ass!”

“Philosophy, he says, when my whole right side is numb and I’m moaning and groaning! I’ve been through the entire medical faculty. They diagnose beautifully, they have your whole disease at their fingertips, but they haven’t the slightest idea how to cure you. I met an enthusiastic young student here. ‘You may die,’ he told me, ‘but you’ll know exactly what disease you’re dying of!’ And then there’s their way of packing people off to specialists! ‘We only diagnose,’ they say, ‘but go and see so-and-so, he’ll cure you.’ The old doctor who treated every kind of illness has vanished altogether, I assure you. Nowadays there are only specialists, and every one of them advertises in the papers. Trouble with your nose? They send you to Paris, where, they say, a European specialist cures noses. In Paris he examines your nose and says: I can cure only your right nostril. I don’t treat the left one, that’s not my specialty. Go to Vienna, there’s a man there who will cure your left nostril. What are you supposed to do? I fell back on folk remedies. A German doctor told me to rub myself with honey and salt in the bathhouse. I went just to get an extra bath, smeared myself from head to foot, and it did me no good whatever. In despair I wrote to Count Mattei in Milan. Bless him, he sent me a book and some drops, and, can you believe it, Hoff’s malt extract cured me! I bought it by accident, drank a bottle and a half, and I was ready to dance. The whole thing vanished. I resolved to write to the newspapers and thank him, moved by gratitude. And can you believe it, that caused no end of trouble. Not one paper would take my letter. ‘It would be very reactionary,’ they said, ‘nobody will believe it. _Le diable n’existe point._ Better stay anonymous,’ they advised. What good is a thank-you letter if it’s anonymous? I joked with the men at the newspaper office. ‘These days it’s reactionary to believe in God,’ I said, ‘but I’m the devil, so people may believe in me.’ ‘We quite understand,’ they said. ‘Who doesn’t believe in the devil? Even so, it won’t do, it could hurt our reputation. As a joke, if you like.’ But I thought, as a joke it wouldn’t be very witty. So it never got printed. And would you believe it, I’m sore about it to this day. My finest feelings, gratitude for one, are literally closed to me, just because of my position in society.”
“Philosophical reflections again?” Ivan snarled with spite.

“Heaven forbid. But a man can’t help complaining now and then. I’m a slandered man. Every minute you reproach me for being stupid. One can tell you’re young. My dear fellow, brains aren’t everything! I have a kind and merry heart by nature. ‘I also write vaudevilles of all sorts.’ You seem to take me for Hlestakov grown old, but my fate is a far more serious one. Before time began, by some decree I could never make sense of, I was fated ‘to deny.’ Yet I’m genuinely good-hearted, and not in the least inclined to negation. ‘No, you must go and deny. Without denial there’s no criticism, and what would a journal be without its column of criticism?’ Without criticism it would be one long ‘hosannah.’ But nothing but hosannah won’t do for life. The hosannah has to be tested in the crucible of doubt, and so on, in the same vein. I don’t meddle in all that, though. I didn’t create it, and I’m not answerable for it. Well, they chose their scapegoat. They made me write the column of criticism, and so life became possible. We understand that comedy. I, for instance, simply ask to be annihilated. No, they tell me, live, because without you there would be nothing. If everything in the universe were reasonable, nothing would ever happen. There would be no events without you, and events there must be. So I serve, against the grain, to bring events about, and I do what’s irrational because I’m ordered to. For all their undoubted intelligence, men take this farce seriously, and that is their tragedy. They suffer, of course ... but then they live. They live a real life, not an imaginary one, because suffering is life. Without suffering, where would the pleasure be? Everything would turn into one endless church service: holy, but dull. And what about me? I suffer, and still I don’t live. I’m the x in an indeterminate equation. I’m a kind of phantom in life, who has lost every beginning and every end, and has even forgotten his own name. You’re laughing—no, you’re not laughing, you’re angry again. You’re always angry. All you care about is intelligence. But I tell you again, I would give up this whole super-stellar life, all the ranks and honors, just to be turned into the soul of a merchant’s wife weighing eighteen stone and to light candles at God’s shrine.”
“So even you don’t believe in God?” said Ivan, with a smile full of hatred.
“What can I say?—that is, if you’re serious—”
“Is there a God or not?” Ivan cried, with the same savage intensity.
“Ah, so you are serious! My dear fellow, On my word, I don’t know. There! I’ve said it!”
“You don’t know, but you see God? No, you’re not someone apart. You’re me, you’re I and nothing more! You’re rubbish, you’re something I’ve dreamed up!”

“Well, if you like, my philosophy is the same as yours, and that would be right. _Je pense, donc je suis_. That much I know for a fact. All the rest, all these worlds, God, even Satan, none of it is proved, as far as I can see. Does it exist on its own, or is it only an emanation of me, a logical development of my ego, which alone has existed forever? But I’d better stop at once, because I suspect you’re about to jump up and beat me.”
“You’d better tell me some anecdote!” said Ivan miserably.

“There’s an anecdote exactly on our subject. Or rather a legend, not an anecdote. You see, you reproach me with unbelief: you say, you see me, yet you don’t believe. But, my dear fellow, I’m not the only one. We’re all in a muddle up there now, and all because of your science. We used to have atoms, five senses, four elements, and somehow everything hung together. There were atoms even in the ancient world. But once we learned that you had discovered the chemical molecule and protoplasm and the devil knows what, we had to lower our crest. It’s a real muddle, and above all there’s superstition and scandal. We have as much scandal among us as you have among you, you know, a little more in fact. And spying, too, since we have our own secret police department that receives private information. Well, this wild legend belongs to our Middle Ages—not yours, ours—and nobody believes it, even among us, except the old ladies of eighteen stone. Not your old ladies, I mean ours. We have everything you have. I’m giving away one of our secrets out of friendship for you, though it’s forbidden. The legend is about Paradise. They say there was once a thinker and philosopher here on earth. He rejected everything: ‘laws, conscience, faith,’ and above all the life to come. He died expecting to go straight into darkness and death, and found a future life in front of him. He was astounded and indignant. ‘This is against my principles!’ he said. And for that he was punished ... that is, you must forgive me, I’m only repeating what I heard myself, it’s only a legend ... he was sentenced to walk a quadrillion kilometers in the dark (we’ve gone metric, you know). When he has finished that quadrillion, the gates of heaven will be opened to him and he’ll be forgiven—”
“And what tortures do you have in the other world, apart from the quadrillion kilometers?” asked Ivan, with a strange eagerness.

“Tortures? Ah, don’t ask. In the old days we had all kinds, but now they’ve gone in mostly for moral punishments—‘the stings of conscience’ and all that nonsense. We picked that up from you, too, from the softening of your manners. And who is better off for it? Only those with no conscience, since how can conscience torture people who haven’t got one? But decent people who do have a conscience and a sense of honor suffer for it. Reforms do nothing but harm when the ground hasn’t been prepared for them, especially institutions copied from abroad! The old fire was better. Well, this man who was condemned to the quadrillion kilometers stood still, looked around, and lay down across the road. ‘I won’t go. I refuse on principle!’ Take the soul of an enlightened Russian atheist, mix it with the soul of the prophet Jonah, who sulked three days and nights in the belly of the whale, and you have the character of that thinker lying across the road.”
“What did he lie on there?”
“Well, I suppose there was something to lie on. You’re not laughing?”
“Bravo!” cried Ivan, with the same strange eagerness. Now he was listening with unexpected curiosity. “Well, is he lying there still?”
“That’s just it, he isn’t. He lay there nearly a thousand years, and then he got up and went on.”

“What an ass!” cried Ivan, laughing nervously, but still seeming to ponder something intently. “Does it make any difference whether he lies there forever or walks the quadrillion kilometers? It would take a billion years to walk it, wouldn’t it?”
“A good deal more than that. I haven’t a pencil and paper or I’d work it out. But he got there long ago, and that’s where the story really starts.”
“What, he got there? But where did he find a billion years to do it?”

“You keep thinking of our present earth! But our present earth may have been repeated a billion times. It dies out, freezes, cracks, breaks into pieces, falls apart into its elements, becomes again ‘the water above the firmament,’ then a comet again, a sun again, and from the sun it turns into earth again. And that same sequence may have been repeated without end, exactly the same down to the last detail, most unseemly and unbearably tedious—”
“Well, well, what happened when he got there?”

“Well, the moment the gates of Paradise opened and he stepped inside, before he’d been there two seconds by his watch (though I think his watch must have dissolved into its elements long before, on the way), he cried out that those two seconds were worth walking not a quadrillion kilometers but a quadrillion of quadrillions, raised to the quadrillionth power! In short, he sang ‘hosannah’ and overdid it so badly that certain persons of lofty ideas there wouldn’t even shake hands with him at first. He’d turned reactionary too fast, they said. The Russian temperament. I repeat, it’s a legend. I give it for what it’s worth. So that’s the kind of ideas we still have about such matters.”

“I’ve caught you!” Ivan cried, with almost childish delight, as if he had at last remembered something. “That anecdote about the quadrillion years, I made it up myself! I was seventeen, still at the high school. I made up that anecdote and told it to a schoolmate named Korovkin, in Moscow.... The anecdote is so typical of me that I couldn’t have taken it from anywhere. I thought I’d forgotten it ... but I recalled it without knowing—I recalled it myself—it wasn’t you telling it! Thousands of things come back unconsciously like that, even to people being led to execution ... it’s come back to me in a dream. You are that dream! You’re a dream, not a living creature!”
“The violence with which you deny my existence,” the gentleman laughed, “convinces me that you do believe in me.”
“Not in the least! I haven’t a hundredth part of a grain of faith in you!”
“But you have a thousandth of a grain. Homeopathic doses, perhaps, are the strongest. Admit that you have faith down to the ten-thousandth of a grain.”
“Not for a minute,” cried Ivan furiously. “But I’d like to believe in you,” he added, oddly.

“Aha! An admission! But I’m good-natured, so I’ll help you out again. Listen, I was the one who caught you, not you me. I told you your own anecdote, which you’d forgotten, on purpose, to destroy your faith in me altogether.”
“You’re lying. You came here to convince me that you exist!”

“Exactly. But hesitating, hanging in suspense, being torn between belief and disbelief—for a conscientious man like you that can be such torture that he’d do better to hang himself and be done with it. I knew you were inclined to believe in me, so I gave you a dose of disbelief with that anecdote. I lead you toward belief and then toward disbelief, by turns, and I have my reasons. It’s the new method. The moment you stop believing in me altogether, you’ll start insisting to my face that I’m no dream but real. I know you. And then I’ll have what I’m after, and it’s an honorable aim. I’ll plant just a tiny seed of faith in you, and it will grow into an oak tree. It will be such an oak that, sitting up in it, you’ll long to join ‘the hermits in the wilderness and the saintly women,’ because that’s what you secretly long for. You’ll live on locusts, you’ll wander off into the wilderness to save your soul!”
“So you’re working for the salvation of my soul, are you, you scoundrel?”
“A man has to do a good deed once in a while. How sour you are!”
“Fool! Did you ever tempt those holy men who lived on locusts and prayed seventeen years in the wilderness, until moss grew all over them?”

“My dear fellow, I’ve done nothing else. You forget the entire world and every other world, and you cling to one such saint, because he’s a very precious diamond. One soul like that, you know, can be worth a whole constellation. We have our own arithmetic. Such a conquest is beyond price! And some of them, on my word, are your equals in education, though you won’t believe it. They can gaze into such depths of belief and disbelief in the same moment that you’d sometimes think they were a hair’s breadth from being ‘turned upside down,’ as the actor Gorbunov puts it.”
“Well, and did you get your nose pulled?”[8]

“My dear fellow,” the visitor said, in a lecturing tone, “it’s better to get away with a pulled nose than to have no nose at all. A poor marquis said as much not long ago (he must have been under some specialist’s care) when he confessed to his spiritual father, a Jesuit. I was there, it was simply delightful. ‘Give me back my nose!’ he cried, beating his breast. ‘My son,’ the priest answered evasively, ‘everything is accomplished by the unfathomable decrees of Providence, and what looks like a misfortune sometimes brings extraordinary benefits, though we can’t see them. If hard fate has taken your nose from you, you have this advantage: no one can ever pull you by it.’ ‘Holy father, that’s no comfort!’ cried the despairing marquis. ‘I’d be glad to have my nose pulled every day of my life, if only it were in its proper place.’ ‘My son,’ sighs the priest, ‘you can’t expect every blessing at once. This is grumbling against Providence, which hasn’t forgotten you even in this. If you complain as you just did, saying you’d be happy to be pulled by the nose for the rest of your life, then your wish has already been granted in a roundabout way. For when you lost your nose, you were led by the nose.’”
“Fool, how stupid!” cried Ivan.

“My dear friend, I only meant to amuse you. But I swear that’s genuine Jesuit casuistry, and I swear it happened word for word as I’ve told it. It happened recently and caused me a great deal of trouble. The poor young man shot himself that same night, as soon as he got home. I stayed beside him to the last moment. Those Jesuit confessionals are honestly my favorite pastime when I’m feeling melancholy. Here’s another story, from just the other day. A little blonde Norman girl of twenty—a plump, artless beauty, enough to make your mouth water—comes to an old priest. She bends down and whispers her sin through the grating. ‘Why, my daughter, have you fallen again already?’ cries the priest. ‘O Sancta Maria, what is this I hear! Not the same man this time! How long is this to go on? Aren’t you ashamed?’ ‘_Ah, mon père_,’ answers the sinner, in tears of repentance, ‘_ça lui fait tant de plaisir, et à moi si peu de peine!_’ Imagine, an answer like that! I recoiled. It was the cry of nature itself, better than innocence, if you like. I forgave her sin on the spot and was turning to leave, but I had to turn back. I heard the priest at the grating arranging to meet her that evening—and he was an old man, hard as flint, yet he fell in an instant! It was nature, the truth of nature, claiming its rights! What, you’re turning up your nose again? Angry again? I can’t find any way to please you—”

“Leave me alone! You’re pounding on my brain like a nightmare that won’t go away,” Ivan moaned miserably, helpless against his apparition. “You bore me, painfully and unbearably. I’d give anything to be rid of you!”

“I say again, lower your expectations, don’t demand ‘everything great and noble’ of me, and you’ll see how well we’ll get along,” said the gentleman, with emphasis. “You’re really angry with me because I haven’t come to you in a red glow, with thunder and lightning and singed wings, but have shown myself in such a modest shape. You’re hurt, first, in your sense of beauty and, second, in your pride. How could so vulgar a devil visit so great a man as you! Yes, there’s that romantic streak in you that Byelinsky used to mock so. I can’t help it, young man. While getting ready to come to you, I did think, as a joke, of appearing as a retired general who had served in the Caucasus, with the star of the Lion and the Sun on my coat. But I was honestly afraid to, because you’d have thrashed me for daring to pin the Lion and the Sun on my coat, instead of at least the Polar Star or Sirius. And you keep saying I’m stupid, but good heavens, I don’t pretend to rival you in intelligence. Mephistopheles told Faust that he wanted evil and did only good. Well, he can say what he pleases; with me it’s just the opposite. I may be the one creature in all creation who loves the truth and truly wishes for good. I was there when the Word, Who died on the Cross, rose up into heaven carrying the soul of the penitent thief on His breast. I heard the glad cries of the cherubim, singing and shouting hosannah, and the thundering rapture of the seraphim that shook heaven and all creation. And I swear to you by everything holy, I longed to join the choir and shout hosannah with them all. The word had almost slipped out, had almost broken from my lips ... you know how sensitive I am, how easily moved by beauty. But common sense—oh, what an unlucky trait in my character—held me back, and I let the moment go by! For what would have happened, I thought, what would have happened after my hosannah? Everything on earth would have gone out at once, and no events could have taken place. And so, purely from a sense of duty and because of my position in society, I had to stifle the good impulse and stay with my nasty job. Somebody else takes all the credit for what’s good, and all that’s left for me is the nastiness. But I don’t envy Him the honor of a life of idle pretense. I’m not ambitious. Why must I, of all creatures in the world, be cursed by every decent person and even kicked? For if I take on human form, I’m bound to take such consequences now and then. I know, of course, that there’s a secret in it, but they won’t tell me the secret for anything. Perhaps, if I saw what it meant, I might bawl out hosannah too, and the indispensable minus would vanish at once, and good sense would rule the whole world. And that, of course, would be the end of everything, even of magazines and newspapers, for who would subscribe to them? I know that at the end of all things I’ll be reconciled. I too will walk my quadrillion and learn the secret. But until then I sulk, and I carry out my destiny, though it goes against my grain—that is, I ruin thousands to save one. How many souls had to be ruined, how many honorable reputations destroyed, for the sake of that one righteous man, Job, over whom they made such a fool of me in the old days! Yes, until the secret is revealed, there are two kinds of truth for me. One is their truth, up there, which I know nothing about so far. The other is my own. And there’s no telling which will turn out better.... Are you asleep?”
“I might well be,” Ivan groaned angrily. “All my stupid ideas—outgrown, threshed out long ago, thrown away like a dead carcass—and you serve them up to me as something new!”
“There’s no pleasing you! And I thought I’d win you over with my literary style. That hosannah in the skies wasn’t bad, was it? And then the ironical tone, _à la_ Heine, eh?”
“No, I was never such a flunkey! How could my soul give birth to a flunkey like you?”

“My dear fellow, I know a most charming, attractive young Russian gentleman, a young thinker and a great lover of literature and art, who wrote a promising poem called _The Grand Inquisitor_. He was the only one I had in mind!”
“I forbid you to speak of _The Grand Inquisitor_,” cried Ivan, red with shame.
“And the _Geological Cataclysm_. Remember that? Now that was a poem!”
“Be quiet, or I’ll kill you!”

“Kill me? No, forgive me, I will speak. I came to give myself that pleasure. Oh, how I love the dreams of my passionate young friends, trembling with eagerness to live! ‘There are new men,’ you decided last spring, when you were getting ready to come here, ‘and they mean to destroy everything and start with cannibalism. Stupid fellows! They didn’t ask my advice! I say nothing needs to be destroyed. All we need to destroy is the idea of God in man, and that’s how we should go about it. That’s where we must begin. Oh, blind race of men, with no understanding! As soon as all men have denied God—and I believe that age will come, like the geological ages—the old view of the universe will collapse of itself, without cannibalism, and what’s more, the old morality will collapse, and everything will start fresh. Men will join together to take from life everything it can give, but only for joy and happiness in this world here. Man will be raised up by a spirit of divine, Titanic pride, and the man-god will appear. Hour by hour he will push back the limits of nature endlessly, by his will and his science, and hour by hour he will feel such lofty joy in doing it that it will make up for all his old dreams of heavenly joys. Everyone will know he is mortal, and will take death proudly and calmly, like a god. His pride will teach him it’s pointless to resent that life is only a moment, and he will love his brother with no thought of reward. Love will be enough only for a moment of life, but the very knowledge that it is momentary will make its flame burn hotter, a flame that is now spent in dreams of eternal love beyond the grave’... and so on and so on in the same style. Charming!”
Ivan sat looking at the floor, his hands pressed over his ears, but he began to tremble all over. The voice went on.

“The question now, my young thinker asked himself, is whether such an age can ever arrive. If it does, everything is decided and humanity is settled for good. But since man’s incurable stupidity means this can’t happen for a thousand years at least, anyone who sees the truth even now may rightly arrange his life as he likes, on the new principles. In that sense ‘all things are lawful’ for him. What’s more, even if that age never arrives, there is in any case no God and no immortality, so the new man may well become the man-god, even if he’s the only one in the whole world. Raised to his new rank, he may cheerfully step over all the barriers of the old morality of the old slave-man, if need be. There is no law for God. Wherever God stands, that place is holy. Wherever I stand will at once be the foremost place ... ‘all things are lawful,’ and that’s the end of it! That’s all very charming. But if you want to cheat, why do you need a moral blessing to do it? But that’s the modern Russian for you. He can’t bring himself to cheat without a moral blessing. He loves truth so much—”

The visitor kept talking, plainly swept along by his own eloquence, getting louder and louder and looking mockingly at his host. But he never got to finish. Ivan suddenly seized a glass from the table and hurled it at the orator.

“_Ah, mais c’est bête enfin_,” cried the other, leaping up from the sofa and shaking drops of tea off himself. “He remembers Luther’s inkstand! He takes me for a dream and throws glasses at a dream! Just like a woman! I suspected you were only pretending to block your ears.”
All at once a loud, insistent knocking came at the window. Ivan sprang up from the sofa.
“Do you hear? You’d better open up,” cried the visitor. “It’s your brother Alyosha, with the most interesting and astonishing news, I’ll bet!”
“Be quiet, you deceiver! I knew it was Alyosha, I felt he was coming, and of course he hasn’t come for nothing. Of course he brings ‘news,’” Ivan exclaimed in a frenzy.
“Open up, open up for him. There’s a snowstorm, and he’s your brother. _Monsieur sait-il le temps qu’il fait? C’est à ne pas mettre un chien dehors_.”

The knocking went on. Ivan tried to rush to the window, but something seemed to shackle his arms and legs. He strained with all his strength to break the chains, but it was no use. The knocking at the window grew louder and louder. At last the chains snapped and Ivan leapt up from the sofa. He looked wildly about him. Both candles had nearly burned down, the glass he had just thrown at his visitor stood in front of him on the table, and the sofa opposite was empty. The knocking on the window frame went on and on, but it was nowhere near as loud as it had seemed in his dream. In fact, it was quite faint.
“It was not a dream! No, I swear it was not a dream, it all happened just now!” cried Ivan. He ran to the window and opened the little hinged pane.
“Alyosha, I told you not to come,” he shouted angrily at his brother. “In two words, what do you want? In two words, do you hear?”
“An hour ago Smerdyakov hanged himself,” Alyosha answered from the yard.
“Go round to the steps, I’ll let you in at once,” said Ivan, going to open the door for Alyosha.
